snp1.12:1.1: The Sutta Nipāta commentary glosses the dangers of intimacy as craving and views.
snp1.12:1.2: The commentary glosses "dust" as passion, aversion, and delusion.
snp1.12:1.4: This verse is quoted in the Milindapañha. The poem as a whole appears to be the same Munigāthā mentioned in King Asoka's Calcutta-Bairāṭ edict.
snp1.12:3.2: The commentary explains "ground," "seed," and "sap" as follows: the aggregates, sense media, and properties form the ground in which the seed of constructive consciousness grows—the consciousness that develops into states of being and birth (compare SN 22:53-55). The sap of that seed is craving and views.
snp1.12:4.1: The commentary glosses "dwellings" (nivesanāni) as states of becoming and birth; the term can also be rendered "entrenchments." See Sn 4:3, note 2.
snp1.12:4.4: The commentary explains "he does not build" as meaning he performs none of the good or bad deeds that give rise to further states of becoming and birth. See Dhp 39, 267, and 412.
snp1.12:6.3: Effluent (āsava) refers to sensual desire, states of becoming, or ignorance—qualities that "flow out" of the mind and defile it. A fourth quality, views, is sometimes added, connecting these with the four floods (ogha), which are identical to the four yokes. See AN 4:10.
snp1.12:8.1: Cv V.1 describes the pillar at a bathing ford as an immovable post, buried deep and standing tall near a bathing place, against which young villagers and boxers would rub their bodies to toughen them. The commentary explains the "extremes" others speak as extremes of praise and criticism, which leave the sage as unmoved as the pillar.
snp1.12:9.1: The commentary glosses "straight as a shuttle" as having a mind unprejudiced by desire, aversion, delusion, or fear. See AN 4:19.
snp1.12:9.3: "Consonant" and "discordant" (sama and visama) draw on musical terminology used across ancient cultures to describe moral quality: discordant intervals or poorly tuned instruments as metaphors for evil, harmonious ones for good. In Pali, sama ("even") described an on-pitch instrument—AN 6:55 has the Buddha telling Ven. Soṇa Kolivisa that a lute sounds right only when its strings are evenly tuned, an image resonant with the middle way. The term samaṇa (monk/contemplative) is traditionally derived from this same root sama, and sāmañña ("evenness") also means the quality of being a contemplative—one always in tune with what is proper. See also DN 2, MN 61, MN 97. Nd II, commenting on Sn 4:2, equates discordant conduct with the ten kinds of misconduct described in MN 41.
snp1.12:12.3: The three intoxications are intoxication with youth, with good health, and with life. See AN 3:39.
snp1.12:13.2: The commentary glosses "ocean" as the way defilement splashes into undesirable destinations, and "flood" as the flow of defilement—sensuality, becoming, views, and ignorance (see SN 45:171). "Such" (tādiṁ) describes one who is unchanging and unaffected by anything, while at the same time undefined.
